sections.h2: What should a Kentucky home seller know before reading the local guides?
sections.html:
Kentucky property sales run through county offices far more than through state ones, so the county where the house sits shapes almost every step. The Commonwealth has 120 counties, and a seller deals with a different set of local officials for assessment, tax collection, deed recording and court matters. Learning who does what saves weeks of phone calls.

The state itself sets the rules in Frankfort. The Department of Revenue publishes the property tax calendar, the General Assembly writes the statutes on landlords, tenants and deed tax, and the county offices carry them out. The guides on this site follow that split: statewide pages explain the law, and county and city pages cover the local office details.

sections.h2: How is Kentucky divided, and why does the county matter so much?
sections.html:
Kentucky is subdivided into 120 counties, a high number for a state of its size. Each county has a county judge/executive and a legislative body called the fiscal court, although that court no longer has judicial functions. The county clerk, sheriff and property valuation administrator are the offices a seller deals with most.

Two counties work differently. Jefferson County and Fayette County have merged their governments with their largest cities, so Louisville Metro and Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government each act as city and county at once. A seller in either place follows one combined set of local rules, and the two counties still exist as subdivisions of the state.

County size varies enormously. The smallest county, Robertson, has around 2,300 residents, while Jefferson has roughly 795,000. Half the counties have fewer than 20,000 people, and 22 have fewer than 10,000.

sections.h2: What are the main regions of Kentucky for housing?
sections.html:
Kentucky splits into several landforms, and the housing stock follows them. Each region has its own mix of farmland, small towns and older housing.

  • The Bluegrass, centered on Lexington and running toward Frankfort and northern Kentucky, holds the horse farms and the fastest growing suburbs.
  • The Pennyroyal Plateau across south central Kentucky includes Bowling Green and Elizabethtown, with cave country and farm parcels.
  • The Western Coal Field around Owensboro, Henderson and Madisonville mixes river towns and mining history.
  • The Jackson Purchase in the far west, around Paducah, sits between the Tennessee and Mississippi rivers.
  • Eastern Kentucky lies largely in Appalachia, with narrow valley lots and steep hillsides.

The state is bordered by rivers on three sides: the Mississippi, the Ohio and the Big Sandy and Tug Fork. Floodplain location can affect insurance and resale, which is why a house near the Ohio River or a creek bottom deserves a flood map check before listing.

sections.h2: What do Kentucky housing and population numbers look like?
sections.html:
QuickFacts lists a 2025 estimate of 4,606,864 people, a gain of 2.2 percent over the 2020 base. Roughly two in three homes are lived in by their owners, and typical values trail the national figure by a wide margin, which shapes what a sale can net after liens and taxes.

sections.h2: Which county office handles which part of a Kentucky property sale?
sections.html:
Four elected offices touch most sales, and each has a distinct job. Calling the wrong one is the most common time waster.

  • The property valuation administrator values every parcel at fair cash value, adds new construction to the roll and takes homestead exemption applications.
  • The sheriff mails and collects the tax bills each fall, then holds them until April 15.
  • The county clerk records deeds, collects the real estate transfer tax, files assessment appeals and takes over unpaid tax bills as certificates of delinquency.
  • The county attorney enforces collection of those delinquent bills and sends the notices that precede a tax sale.

For a title question, ask the clerk. For an assessment or exemption question, ask the valuation administrator. For a balance owed this year, ask the sheriff, and after April 15 ask the clerk.

sections.h2: What does a seller pay at closing in Kentucky besides the loan payoff?
sections.html:
The person signing the deed owes a transfer tax of $0.50 on every $500 of declared value or fraction of it, and the clerk takes it at recording. A house priced at the $205,600 median would owe about $206. Foreclosure transfers and surrenders in lieu of foreclosure fall outside the tax, and so do spouse-to-spouse deeds and nominal parent-to-child deeds.

Property tax is the other line item. Bills are based on the assessment as of January 1 and paid to the sheriff from October onward. Ask the sheriff whether the current year bill is paid before you list, and ask the clerk whether any older certificate of delinquency is on file against the parcel.

sections.h2: How do tax dates and penalties work across the state?
sections.html:
One collection pattern covers the whole state, with a stretched version for counties that mail late. A 2 percent discount applies through November 1, the face amount through December 31, then 5 percent in January and 21 percent from February 1 until April 15. After that date the bill sits with the clerk, and monthly interest of 1 percent plus clerk and attorney fees start adding up.

The state also sets a single real property rate each year. The 2025 figure, announced by the Department of Revenue, was 10.6 cents on each $100 of assessed value, a drop from 10.9. Counties, cities, school boards and special districts layer on their own levies, so identical houses in different taxing districts can receive quite different bills.

sections.h2: What should a landlord or heir know about the local rules?
sections.html:
Rental rules differ by place. The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies only where a city, county or urban-county government adopted it as written, and a 2024 statute bars local landlord-tenant ordinances that conflict with state law. In Jefferson County, a separate statute limits some new leases in traditional single-family zones unless the owner lives on the lot.

For inherited houses, the practical steps are the same in every county: confirm who holds title, check the tax bill status with the sheriff and clerk, and find out whether a homestead exemption was in place for the deceased owner. The exemption is tied to the person, so a successor has to apply on their own account if they qualify.

sections.h2: Which natural hazards affect Kentucky homes?
sections.html: Flooding and tornadoes are the two recurring events in the state record. The Ohio River flood of 1937 reached across the state, the April 1974 tornado outbreak hit statewide, and a tornado outbreak on May 15 and 16, 2025 caused 19 deaths across Kentucky and six other states. A house with storm or flood damage can usually still be sold as is, but the buyer and any lender will want to see repair records and insurance claims.

faqs.q: How many counties does Kentucky have?
faqs.a: Kentucky has 120 counties. Jefferson is the most populous, with about 795,000 people, and Robertson is the smallest, with about 2,300. Pike is the largest by area at roughly 788 square miles.

faqs.q: Who do I call first when selling an inherited house in Kentucky?
faqs.a: Begin at the clerk's office, which records deeds and holds overdue tax bills. Then ask the property valuation administrator about a homestead exemption, and ask the sheriff whether this year's bill has been paid.

faqs.q: Does the same property tax calendar apply in every Kentucky county?
faqs.a: In outline, yes. Most sheriffs start collecting October 1 and give the discount through November 1, and anything unpaid goes to the clerk on April 15. A county that mails after November 1 allows 30 days for each stage.

faqs.q: Is there a state tax on transferring a deed in Kentucky?
faqs.a: Yes. The seller owes $0.50 per $500 of value when the deed is filed with the clerk. Transfers by foreclosure or by surrender in lieu of it are excluded.

faqs.q: Are Louisville and Lexington handled differently from other places?
faqs.a: Their city and county governments are merged into Louisville Metro and Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government, so local rules come from one body. The two counties still exist as subdivisions of the state.
